claim: Erd1 is functionally related to genes known to mediate glycosylation and transport events at the ER and Golgi based on genetic interaction profile analysis.
source: Our analysis indicated that Erd1 is functionally related to genes known to mediate glycosylation and transport events at the ER and Golgi.
evidence: The claim is supported by SAFE and PSN analysis of genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: erd1Δ mutant cells exhibit sensitivity to tunicamycin, an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation.
source: as well as tunicamycin, an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental growth assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The observations in erd1Δ mutant are in agreement with previously reported defects in Golgi-based CPY and invertase modifications.
source: These observations are also in agreement with the reported defects in Golgi based CPY and invertase modifications in the erd1 mutant isolated from the HDEL-invertase screen Hardwick and Pelham, 1990.

claim: Endogenously tagged Erd1-mNeongreen predominantly co-localizes with the early-Golgi marker Mnn9.
source: Endogenously tagged Erd1-mNeongreen predominantly co-localized with the early-Golgi marker, Mnn9, and to some extent with the medial-Golgi marker, Gea2, suggesting its function in early to medial Golgi compartments (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Endogenously tagged Erd1-mNeongreen co-localizes to some extent with the medial-Golgi marker Gea2.
source: Endogenously tagged Erd1-mNeongreen predominantly co-localized with the early-Golgi marker, Mnn9, and to some extent with the medial-Golgi marker, Gea2, suggesting its function in early to medial Golgi compartments (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Erd1 functions in early to medial Golgi compartments.
source: Endogenously tagged Erd1-mNeongreen predominantly co-localized with the early-Golgi marker, Mnn9, and to some extent with the medial-Golgi marker, Gea2, suggesting its function in early to medial Golgi compartments (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-localization data with early and medial Golgi markers.

claim: Vps74 is a peripheral membrane protein that acts as the cytosolic receptor for COPI recycling.
source: Vps74 is a peripheral membrane protein that acts as the cytosolic receptor for COPI recycling Schmitz et al., 2008; Tu et al., 2012; Tu et al., 2008; Welch et al., 2021; Rizzo et al., 2021.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: SAFE analysis on global genetic interactions indicates a robust functional overlap between Erd1 and Vps74.
source: Furthermore, SAFE analysis on the global genetic interactions indicated a robust functional overlap between Erd1 and Vps74 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SAFE analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The hygromycin sensitivity of erd1Δ and vps74Δ mutants resembles a defect similar to the loss of multiple glycosyltransferases.
source: their sensitivity to hygromycin resembled a defect similar to the loss of multiple glycosyltransferases (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of Erd1 and Vps74 manifests in a defect in recycling of the same subset of Golgi glycosyltransferases.
source: Indeed, loss of Erd1 and Vps74 manifested in a defect in recycling of the same subset of Golgi glycosyltransferases.
evidence: The claim is supported by the localization data of multiple glycosyltransferases shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All tested glycosyltransferases that are Erd1-dependent contain the cytosolic motif previously reported to require Vps74 binding.
source: All the tested glycosyltransferases that were Erd1-dependent also contained the cytosolic motif previously reported to require Vps74 binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) Tu et al., 2008.

claim: In the absence of Vps74, Erd1 is not incorporated into COPI recycling vesicles and is instead delivered to the vacuole.
source: This suggests that in the absence of Vps74, Erd1 itself is not incorporated into COPI recycling vesicles and is instead delivered to the vacuole.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Erd1 is mislocalized to the vacuole in vps74Δ mutant.

claim: Erd1 is not required for recruitment of Vps74 to the Golgi.
source: Thus, whereas Erd1 is not required for recruitment of Vps74, it appears to be required for the function of Vps74 at the Golgi.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Vps74 localizes normally to the Golgi in erd1Δ mutant.

claim: Erd1 is required for the function of Vps74 at the Golgi.
source: Thus, whereas Erd1 is not required for recruitment of Vps74, it appears to be required for the function of Vps74 at the Golgi.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Vps74 localizes normally but glycosyltransferases are still mislocalized in erd1Δ mutant.

claim: The Vps74-dependent pathway recycles single pass type II membrane proteins such as glycosyltransferases.
source: These observations also indicate that the Vps74-dependent pathway recycles single pass type II membrane proteins such as glycosyltransferases as well as multi-pass transmembrane proteins such as Erd1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both glycosyltransferases and Erd1 require Vps74 for proper localization.

claim: The Vps74-dependent pathway recycles multi-pass transmembrane proteins such as Erd1.
source: These observations also indicate that the Vps74-dependent pathway recycles single pass type II membrane proteins such as glycosyltransferases as well as multi-pass transmembrane proteins such as Erd1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Erd1 is mislocalized to the vacuole in vps74Δ mutant.

claim: Overexpression of Erd1 in the vps74Δ mutant partially suppresses the hygromycin sensitivity of the vps74Δ mutant.
source: Overexpression of Erd1 in the vps74Δ mutant partially suppressed the hygromycin and temperature sensitivity of the vps74Δ mutant (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Overexpression of Erd1 in the vps74Δ mutant partially suppresses the temperature sensitivity of the vps74Δ mutant.
source: Overexpression of Erd1 in the vps74Δ mutant partially suppressed the hygromycin and temperature sensitivity of the vps74Δ mutant (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Overexpression of Vps74 in the erd1Δ mutant severely inhibits its growth fitness.
source: In contrast, overexpression of Vps74 in the erd1Δ mutant, severely inhibited its growth fitness (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2I (note: there appears to be a typo in the manuscript as Figure 2I is referenced but Figure 2H shows the relevant data).

claim: The toxicity of Vps74 overexpression in erd1Δ mutant is specifically due to maintenance of Vps74 expressing plasmid.
source: This toxicity was specifically due to maintenance of Vps74 expressing plasmid, as the growth was normal on rich media with no selection for the plasmid.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that growth is normal on non-selective media.

claim: Mutations in Vps74 that disrupt COPI binding (vps74 R6-8A) alleviate the toxicity of Vps74 overexpression in erd1Δ mutant.
source: Mutations in Vps74 that disrupt COPI binding (vps74 R6-8A) or oligomerization (vps74Δ201–204) alleviated the toxicity (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mutations in Vps74 that disrupt oligomerization (vps74Δ201–204) alleviate the toxicity of Vps74 overexpression in erd1Δ mutant.
source: Mutations in Vps74 that disrupt COPI binding (vps74 R6-8A) or oligomerization (vps74Δ201–204) alleviated the toxicity (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Overexpression of Vps74 in the erd1Δ mutant results in futile Vps74-COPI complexes that reduce the level of free COPI available for Golgi function.

evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the toxicity data.

claim: The erd1Δsec21-1 double mutant exhibits a synthetic growth defect even at permissive temperature.
source: Consistent with this, the erd1Δsec21-1 mutant, defective in Erd1 and COPI function, exhibited a similar synthetic growth defect even at permissive temperature (Figure 2I).

claim: There is significant interdependence between Erd1 and Vps74 in the COPI-mediated intra-Golgi recycling of specific Golgi cargos.
source: Collectively, these observations indicate significant interdependence between Erd1 and Vps74 in the COPI-mediated intra-Golgi recycling of specific Golgi cargos.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective genetic and biochemical data presented.

claim: Erd1 has previously been proposed to play a role in Golgi ion homeostasis by transporting phosphate from the Golgi lumen to the cytosol.
source: Erd1 has previously been proposed to play a role in Golgi ion homeostasis by transporting phosphate from the Golgi lumen to the cytosol Snyder et al., 2017.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The erd1Δ mutant leads to loss of phosphate via exocytosis.
source: The erd1Δ mutant led to loss of phosphate (Pi) via exocytosis, and required 1.5-fold higher concentration of Pi in the media for 50% maximal growth as compared to wild type Snyder et al., 2017.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The erd1Δ mutant requires 1.5-fold higher concentration of Pi in the media for 50% maximal growth compared to wild type.
source: The erd1Δ mutant led to loss of phosphate (Pi) via exocytosis, and required 1.5-fold higher concentration of Pi in the media for 50% maximal growth as compared to wild type Snyder et al., 2017.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Deletion of Pmr1 results in a similar Gas1 glycosylation defect as loss of Erd1 or Vps74.
source: As expected, deletion of Pmr1 results in a similar Gas1 glycosylation defect as loss of Erd1 or Vps74 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Supplementing the media with Ca2+ or Mn2+ rescues the glycosylation defect observed in pmr1Δ mutant.
source: However, while supplementing the media with Ca2+ or Mn2+ rescued the glycosylation defect observed in pmr1Δ mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Supplementing the media with 50-fold higher Pi does not rescue the glycosylation defect in the erd1Δ mutant.
source: supplementing the media with even 50-fold higher Pi did not rescue the glycosylation defect in the erd1Δ mutant.

claim: Despite the glycosylation defect, pmr1Δ mutant has no defect in the localization and recycling of Kre2.
source: Importantly, despite the glycosylation defect, pmr1Δ mutant had no defect in the localization and recycling of Kre2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).

claim: While Erd1 may play a role in phosphate homeostasis at the early Golgi, it has a distinct role in glycosyltransferase recycling.
source: Therefore, while it is possible that Erd1 plays a role in phosphate homeostasis at the early Golgi, our data support a distinct role of Erd1 in also being required for glycosyltransferase recycling.

claim: Erd1 directly interacts with Vps74.

claim: Erd1 directly interacts with glycosyltransferases.

claim: Fluorescence complementation is not detectable between tagged Erd1 and the oligomerization defective vps74 Δ201–204 mutant.
